components.coverage: Nix derivation/build-dependency matching for every scan-classified public package on all supported systems; default is an alias of hey.
Pinned cmd, judge, posix-spawn, sh and spork sources are referenced by the inventory and Hey graph. Generic package names do not guarantee upstream advisory matching.

Separate public npm registry audit of the committed lockfile with development dependencies omitted; native Node dependencies also appear in Nix graphs. Node's bundled Undici/global fetch and linked OpenSSL are outside the npm lock audit.
Effective default packages of five representative synthetic Linux service configurations on both Linux architectures; no system closure or service execution.
The actual module's default Emacs package is a Nix scan root on all systems. Doom configuration and source pins are inventoried; the resolved Lisp/grammar graph is excluded.
Cilium chart/Gateway API pins and recipe sources are inventoried. K3s/Cilium image layers and running cluster image choices are not inspected.
Codegraph's public package version is scanned; embedded libraries in the upstream binary require a separate upstream SBOM/source review.

exclusions.reason: Complete Doom Lisp and Tree-sitter inventory requires the actual selected Doom configuration and evaluation/build prerequisites; this runner never relaxes the IFD guard.
Derivation matching does not inspect OCI layers, chart-selected images, sidecars or runtime cluster images; digest-bound image scanning remains separate.

Prebuilt Codegraph, Node's bundled Undici/global fetch and other vendored/bundled code may not expose individual library versions to NVD matching; a scanned parent or clean npm lock is not coverage of every embedded component.
Private hosts, inputs, closures, credentials, overrides, arbitrary workstation packages, Homebrew/external tools and consumer-selected configurations are never public scan targets.
Humanizer/taste are data-only; hey-janet-lib is included through Hey. These do not receive independent package-name scans.
Vulnix uses package-name/version and CVE-patch heuristics; npm uses registry advisories. Database freshness, backports, unsupported ecosystems and reachability need review.
